passage: Fear is a common part of human life, and many people try to deal with it in different ways.
A teacher once held a Fear Party for her students, encouraging them to talk about their fears.
This idea was seen as helpful for people of all ages to share their worries.
Dr. George W. Crane, a medical writer, believed that group confessionals could reduce neurotic ailments significantly.
He noted that many people visit doctors not because of physical illness, but because they need someone to listen to their troubles.
Some doctors report that most of their patients worry about things that never happen or events they cannot control.
A few worry about their health when there is no real problem.
Others are concerned about friends or family who are perfectly capable of taking care of themselves.
Only a small percentage of worries are based on real issues that need to be addressed.
Despite this, people continue to feel anxious and search for ways to escape their fears.
They spend large sums of money on fortune tellers, gambling, liquor, and entertainment.
These activities are meant to distract from their inner tensions.
A visitor from another country once said that Americans seemed sad, but the real word was jittery.
This shows how much anxiety affects people in modern society.
Places like amusement parks and nightclubs offer loud and constant entertainment, but many people go there to avoid their fears.
Blaise Pascal once wrote that this need for distraction is a sign of deep misery and fear.
As global tensions rise, especially with nuclear threats, fear is becoming more widespread.
Some people suggest that fear parties or group confessionals might help, but it is unclear if these will be effective.
Many fears are already visible in the news and in public discussions.
Perhaps talking about fears is not the solution, but it is hard to know what else to do.
Meanwhile, those who wish to take advantage of fear will likely find ways to use it for their own purposes.

passage: Richard became deeply interested in religion when he was twelve years old.
He began reading works by St. Augustine, Aquinas, Lao-tse, and Confucius, among others.
His mother, noticing his fascination, bought him the Zend-Avesta and a small image of the Indian god Acala.
Later, she surprised him with a copy of The Book of the Dead, which he greatly appreciated.
Richard spent hours reading the book and kept it close for many years.
By the time he was fourteen, he had developed strong religious views and once told his parents, 'There is only one god.'
His father responded with a grin, but Richard remained serious and spoke little after that.
As he grew older, his interest in formal religion waned, and he shifted his focus to Asian affairs.
Despite this change, he still carried the image of Acala and the books he had collected.
When he moved to New York to study, he lived a solitary life and developed a thorough but bookish knowledge of Asian culture.
He was awarded a fellowship to study in Tokyo and returned home briefly before leaving the country.
During his visit, his mother asked if he still had The Book of the Dead.
He lied and said, 'Yes,' but in truth, he had burned all his religious books in the basement furnace of his New York apartment.
He had carefully dusted each one before placing them in the fire, trembling as he did so.
Afterward, he ran from the basement and cried in his room.
Richard left America with only his clothes, the biwa he had been learning to play, and the image of Acala.
On the ship to Japan, he played the biwa, trying to recreate an ancient Japanese melody.
One night, he stole from his cabin and dropped the instrument into the ocean.
The darkness and the noise of the sea made it impossible to see or hear the biwa fall.
In Tokyo, Richard found a new kind of companionship with an American student named Charlotte.
She was lively and curious, and she gradually helped him open up to others.
He attended small gatherings at her apartment and, though he rarely spoke, he appreciated her company.
Charlotte once told a story about seeing a naked man in a pool at Ryusenji, but Richard found her tone too casual for his taste.
He preferred their private conversations, where he could feel more understood.
Despite his growing social connections, Richard remained introspective and continued to carry the image of Acala with him.
His journey from solitary study to cautious engagement with others marked a quiet but significant transformation in his life.

options.A: Richard completely rejected all religious beliefs when he arrived in Tokyo.
options.B: After burning his books, Richard was emotionally at peace and fully embraced his new life in Japan.
options.C: Richard became very outgoing and started speaking freely with others in Tokyo.
options.D: Richard no longer had the biwa when he arrived in Tokyo.

passage: Curt returned from the livery stable and quickly realized that Jess's horse was still missing.
He climbed through a back window and dropped to the ground, careful not to be seen.
The absence of the buckskin could mean Diane's information was wrong, but Curt decided not to interpret it that way.
He believed Jess would want a way to escape if needed, so his horse was likely nearby.
From the back of the barn, it was easy to reach Black's house without using the street.
Curt approached cautiously and watched the house for several minutes from the safety of a grove of trees.
A light was on in the front room, but the curtains were drawn, blocking any view inside.
He moved around the house and found a barn out back, where he could hear horses moving around.
There was no lock on the door, only an iron hook, which he easily unfastened.
He stepped inside and pulled the door shut behind him, staying in the darkness and listening carefully.
The only sound was the scrape of a shod hoof on the floor.
He moved forward slowly, his left hand out in front of him, and came to a wooden partition.
The smell of horses was strong, and he could hear the crunch of grain being eaten.
He found a match in his pocket and lit it, revealing two horses in the barn: a sway-backed dun and Jess Crouch's buckskin.
Curt snuffed out the match and realized that Jess was in the house, presumably with Stacey Black.
Curt wanted to get Jess alone, without interference from anyone, even someone as spineless as the store owner.
He studied the situation for a few seconds and thought of a way to achieve his goal.
Reaching across the side of the stall, he slapped the buckskin on the rump, signaling the start of his plan.
The sound of the slap echoed faintly in the stillness, and the horse shifted uneasily in its stall.
Curt remained motionless, his eyes adjusting to the dim light and scanning the shadows for any sign of movement.
He could feel the cold seeping into his boots and the tension in his muscles as he prepared for what came next.
The silence in the barn was oppressive, broken only by the occasional rustle of hay or the soft breathing of the animals.
He considered the risks of his plan, knowing that any mistake could alert Jess or Black to his presence.
Still, the need to act outweighed the fear, and Curt steeled himself for the confrontation ahead.

passage: Gavin Maxwell’s book Ring of Bright Water tells the story of a man who lives in a remote Scottish village and forms a deep bond with an otter named Mijbil.
The setting is Camusfearna, a place with long fjords, few people, and a wild, natural landscape.
Maxwell finds peace and connection in this isolated location, surrounded by dolphins, swans, and stags.
He gradually builds a home from the remnants of the sea and the land.
Over time, the seasons change and the environment shifts, but the presence of Mijbil brings joy and meaning to his life.
Mijbil is no ordinary otter; he is curious, playful, and full of strange habits.
He likes to sleep in beds, open drawers, and play with small objects like marbles.
One day, Mijbil climbs to the top of a cliff and waits for Maxwell to rescue him, showing a deep trust in his human companion.
Maxwell writes about the emotional bond they share, which grows stronger with each passing day.
The otter’s actions reflect a kind of innocence and loyalty that Maxwell finds deeply moving.
Mijbil also interacts with others, including a second person who becomes part of their small world.
The three of them form a kind of family, with Mijbil at the center.
However, the idyllic life ends when Mijbil dies, a tragic event that leaves Maxwell heartbroken.
The cause of Mijbil’s death is not fully explained, but it is clear that it was sudden and unexpected.
In the aftermath, Maxwell feels a sense of loss and emptiness, but he is not ready to give up on the life he has built.

passage: In 1961, Governor John A. Notte, Jr. of Rhode Island proclaimed the week of April 29th to May 7th as Rhode Island Heritage Week.
The theme was 'Independence and Union,' marking the 185th anniversary of the state's declaration of independence in 1776.
On May 4 of that year, the General Assembly became the first free republic in the New World.
This year also marked the centennial of the start of the Civil War, and the state honored the first Rhode Island Volunteers who answered President Lincoln's call for help in 1861.
These soldiers were the only fully trained and equipped regiment available at the time.
On April 30, ceremonies were held at the Dexter Training Grounds in Providence to commemorate their departure.
The governor also announced a military and civic parade on Independence Day, starting in West Warwick and ending at the Greene Homestead.
During Heritage Week, many historic sites, gardens, museums, and libraries were open to the public.
Governor Notte urged citizens to visit these places and learn about their state's rich history.
In the same year, he also issued a proclamation for Armed Forces Day on May 20th.
This day celebrated the 14th anniversary of the unification of the U.S. Armed Forces under the National Security Act of 1947.
The governor emphasized that national defense is a shared responsibility and a crucial investment in peace and freedom.
He quoted the President, stating that a strong military ensures peace because it prevents the need for actual conflict.
Armed Forces Day was described as an opportunity for Americans to honor those who serve, including those who made the supreme sacrifice.
The governor called for citizens to respect the military and recognize their role in protecting the nation's liberty.
He reminded people that freedom depends on the courage and dedication of service members.
Through these proclamations, Governor Notte aimed to educate the public about the state's history and the importance of national unity and defense.
He encouraged all Rhode Islanders to participate in the events and reflect on the values that shaped their country.
These proclamations were signed with the official seal of the state and marked as significant moments in Rhode Island's history.
In addition, Governor Notte proclaimed May 22nd as National Maritime Day, commemorating the 1819 voyage of the S.S. 'Savannah,' the first successful transatlantic crossing under steam propulsion.
This day honored the contributions of American merchant mariners, who played a vital role in both peace and war as the 'Fourth Arm of Defense.'
The governor also recognized the Miss Rhode Island Pageant as an important event in promoting youth development and community engagement across the state.

passage: The land stretched endlessly before them, dry and hot, like a place forgotten by rain.
Its cracked earth baked under the relentless sun, offering no relief from the heat.

They plodded forward as if burdened by the weight of the arid landscape.
The sun burned fiercely, turning the air into something thick and hard to breathe.
A molten glare singed their eyelids and left them an angry crimson.
Dust filled the sky and settled on every surface, making it hard to see and even harder to move.
The suffocating air sapped their strength and strained their nerves to snapping.
Ben Prime, the man in charge, felt the heat in every part of his body.
The sweat dried on his skin in salt-edged patches, and his cracked, black-burned lips ached with every movement.
He tried to encourage the oxen with loud commands, but his voice came out rough and dry.
The effort of moving caused a sharp pain in his cracked lips.
He removed his hat to let the trapped sweat cut rivulets through the dust film upon his gaunt face.
But the dust only made it worse, clinging stubbornly to his skin and eyes.
The water was running low, and each drop had to be used carefully.
They could no longer afford the luxury of the canvas sweat bag that cooled it by evaporation.
He poured some into a dipper and handed it to his wife, who sat quietly at the back of the wagon.
Her dark eyes were baleful as they met his, filled with a simmering anger.
She took the water but did not look happy, her expression tight with resentment.
She drank it slowly, as if savoring the bitterness of the moment.
Her dark eyes were angry, and her voice was sharp when she spoke.
Her words carried a fire that had been growing for days, like a coiled spring ready to snap.
'What happens when there's no more water?' she asked, her tone smoldering with frustration.
The question hung in the heavy air like a threat.
Her words carried a fire that had been growing for days, and Ben tried to stay calm.
He could feel the tension in her, a heat that burned just beneath her surface.
'We can dig for water,' he said, his voice steady despite the strain in his limbs.
His homely face tilted toward the dry bed of the river as if searching for hope in the dust.
'It might not be clean, but we can boil it,' he continued, his tone patient and measured.

passage: Ambiguity in language is a common source of confusion and humor, occurring when words or sentences can be interpreted in more than one way.
Many famous people have commented on this issue, including Ben Franklin, who once said, 'Clearly spoken, Mr. Fogg.
You explain English by Greek.'
This quote illustrates how difficult it can be to communicate clearly.
A similar sentiment was echoed by Richard Brinsley Sheridan, who noted that interpreters are often the hardest to understand.
Writers sometimes create confusion by repeating phrases in a confusing way.
An example is a conversation where someone asks, 'Did you or did you not say what I said you said, because Jane said you never said what I said?'
This type of repetition makes it hard to follow the meaning.
A woman writing Christmas cards questioned her husband about whether they should send cards this year.
Her sentence becomes so long and repetitive that it creates a confusing loop.
This showcases how even well-intentioned communication can go wrong.
A girl once wrote to a friend that she had told Bill not to reconsider her decision not to change her mind.
Bill misunderstood her message completely.
Politicians are often caught in ambiguous situations.
A reporter asked a politician about his denial of having retracted a contradiction.
The politician struggled to respond clearly.
Lincoln once refused to explain further, saying, 'I fear explanations explanatory of things explained.'
This highlights how even experienced leaders can be confused by unclear language.
Misplaced modifiers are another type of ambiguity, occurring when a word is placed in a sentence in a way that changes its meaning.
An example is the question: 'Now can you tell me who was drunk — the man, his wife, or me?'
The answer depends on how the sentence is read.
This trick was used by vaudeville comedians in their jokes, such as the gag asking, 'There's a man outside with a wooden leg named Smith.'
The follow-up question is, 'What's the name of his other leg?'
This plays on the listener's confusion.
Radio and journalism also use misplaced modifiers for humor, as seen when a reporter asked, 'Do you see that pretty girl standing next to the car with slacks on?'
The listener misunderstood the sentence and looked for the car in slacks.
Cartoonists have also used this type of trick in their work, as seen in a cartoon where a father says he left 'my daughter's handbag and my wife's behind.'

passage: The Oslo meeting of NATO Foreign Ministers brought about a significant shift in the alliance’s atmosphere, marked by more open and honest discussions among member states.
This change was particularly noticeable between nations with historical disagreements, such as those with colonial ties and those without.
The meeting allowed for a better understanding of each country’s challenges, especially regarding the tensions in Africa and the emotional and intellectual divides within the alliance.
Portugal, which had previously been on the verge of withdrawing from the NATO Council due to criticism of its Angola policy, showed a more relaxed attitude during the meeting.
Although the country’s position remained unchanged, the absence of conflict was a welcome sign for the alliance.
Canada, however, remained somewhat isolated from the general consensus reached by other NATO members.
Despite public demonstrations in Norway against nuclear weapons, the country’s stance aligned more closely with the NATO line.
On the other hand, U.S. leadership was less prominent than expected, with Secretary of State Dean Rusk’s speeches described as inconclusive.
Some diplomats suggested that this was due to the new administration not yet having fully defined its foreign policy.
The U.S. delegation was perceived as cautious, more willing to listen than to assert a clear stance on global issues.
Nevertheless, Rusk reaffirmed the U.S. commitment to NATO and announced that five nuclear submarines would be made available for the alliance.
He also reiterated a strong warning to the Soviet Union about any further aggression in Berlin.
The meeting also emphasized the need for deeper political cooperation within NATO, the use of the OECD for aid coordination, and the strengthening of conventional military forces.
This last point, known as the 'threshold,' is expected to be a major challenge for the alliance in the coming months.
As the meeting concluded, the focus shifted to the Kennedy administration’s foreign policy, particularly regarding Laos and Cuba.
The administration was considering a Geneva conference on Laos, where it hoped to prevent the country from becoming a base for Communist attacks on neighboring states.
However, no clear formula had been developed to prevent a Communist-dominated government in Laos.
The U.S. was also shifting its stance on the Laos cease-fire, favoring a de facto agreement over strict verification.
This policy change was attributed to the administration’s response to earlier mistakes made under the previous leadership.
Meanwhile, political criticism from within the U.S. grew, with former Vice President Nixon calling for a tougher approach toward the Soviet Union.
Republicans in Congress expressed frustration over what they saw as overly conciliatory policies.
They avoided direct confrontation with the Kennedy administration, believing that unity was more important at the moment.
In addition, a group of 70 educators from leading universities urged the administration to seek diplomatic solutions in Cuba rather than supporting exile invasions.
They recommended a resumption of trade and diplomatic relations with the Castro regime.
Nixon, while opposing intervention in Cuba, suggested a clear warning against further arms shipments to the island.
The Kennedy administration’s policies, especially in the wake of the Cuban Missile Crisis and military setbacks in Laos, were being closely scrutinized.
Critics questioned whether the administration’s early decisions had been effective in countering Communist aggression.
Despite these challenges, the administration had initially shown a balanced approach that respected both diplomatic and military strategies.
Efforts were also made to strengthen alliances and avoid further provocations with the Soviet Union.
However, the path forward remained uncertain as the administration navigated complex global tensions and domestic political pressures.

passage: The land stretched endlessly before them, dry and hot, like a place forgotten by rain.

He removed his hat to let the sweat cool his face, but the dust only made it worse.
The water was running low, and each drop had to be used carefully.

She took the water but did not look happy.
Her dark eyes were angry, and her voice was sharp when she spoke.

Her words carried a fire that had been growing for days.
Ben tried to stay calm, even though he could feel the tension in her.
He looked at the dry ground and suggested that they could dig for water if they had to.
'It might not be clean,' he said, 'but we can boil it.'
She shook her head, her expression full of doubt and barely contained frustration.
'You don’t even know where we are going,' she said, her voice laced with accusation.
'The map doesn’t show a place like this, and the wheels are almost broken from the heat and dust.'
The wooden wheels creaked and groaned with every step, their iron bands warping in the relentless heat.
They had no idea where they were, and the map had led them into an unknown and unforgiving terrain.
Ben looked at the dry riverbed and thought about the possibility of water hidden beneath the dirt.
He believed they could find it if they tried, though the effort would be exhausting.
But he also knew that his wife had been carrying a quiet anger, like something smoldering just below the surface.
Her silence was as powerful as her words, and it spoke of a growing divide between them.
The journey had tested them both, and the heat had made every moment feel longer than it was.
Still, Ben did not give up.
He believed in the future, even when it was unclear and uncertain.
He believed in the land, even when it seemed to have no mercy and no promise.
And he believed in the strength it would take to survive, no matter what the day might bring.

passage: The construction of the Hotei begins with a thorough study of the detailed drawings provided.
The first step involves laying out the six frames and the transom on a level floor.
Each frame is outlined in a different-colored chalk to help detect any obvious mistakes during the layout process.
The transom frame is constructed first, with the joints lapped, glued, and fastened using one-inch, No.
12 Stronghold nails.
After notching it for the keelson, chines, and battens, a half-inch plywood transom is attached with glue and the same type of nails.
All frames are butted at the joints and reinforced with 3/8-inch plywood gussets glued and nailed on each side.
These gussets are also secured with one-inch, No.
12 nails.

The frames are notched only for the keelson and the chines to avoid unnecessary weakening and the need for limber holes, and the frames do not come into direct contact with the plywood planking at any point during the construction.
After the frames and transom are complete, the jig is erected.
This is a crucial step because any misalignment at this stage could lead to progressively worse misalignment in the hull.
All members of the jig must be parallel, vertical, and level.
Once the frames and transom are set up on the jig and temporarily braced, a three-inch-wide piece of mahogany is placed between the first and second frames below the keelson line.
The frames are glued and screwed to this piece, and the joints are reinforced on each side with small blocks set in resin-saturated Fiberglas cloth and nailed.
The laminated stem and keelson are spliced over this piece.
The keelson, made from two three-inch widths of mahogany, is then installed next.
Throughout the construction, one-inch mahogany is used for all framing, and it is cut to size from planks using a table saw.
In addition to the wood, silicon bronze Stronghold nails and Weldwood resorcinol glue are used extensively for assembly.
These materials ensure a strong and durable build.

The press played a key role in shaping public opinion.

Despite his reassurances, Eisenhower struggled with the weight of the decision.

His confidence in his ability to lead was tested by the doubts and fears of those around him.

Ultimately, Eisenhower’s decision to run for re-election became a defining moment in American political history.

passage: In the United States, most taxpayers must file their income tax returns by April 15 each year.
This date is the final deadline for those who use the calendar year ending on December 31.
If the due date falls on a weekend or holiday, the deadline is extended to the next business day.
Taxpayers who use a fiscal year, which ends on the last day of any month other than December, must file by the 15th day of the fourth month after the close of their tax year.
For example, if a taxpayer's fiscal year ends on June 30, their return is due on October 15.
If a taxpayer realizes they should have itemized deductions instead of using the standard deduction, they can file an amended return.
The words 'amended return' must be clearly written across the top of the form.
Similarly, if they itemized but should have used the standard deduction, they can also correct this by filing an amended return within the allowed time.
These changes must be made before the statute of limitations for filing a claim for refund expires.
Nonresident aliens living in Canada or Mexico who earn wages in the U.S. may be subject to tax withholding, just like U.S. citizens.
Their tax returns are due on April 16.
However, if their income is not subject to withholding, their return is due on June 15.
Nonresident aliens in Puerto Rico also have a deadline of June 15.
These deadlines apply to those using the calendar year; for those with a fiscal year, the due date is the 15th day of the sixth month after the tax year ends.
If a taxpayer dies, the executor or legal representative must file the final return by the 15th day of the fourth month following the close of the deceased's tax year.
For example, if a taxpayer who used the calendar year died on June 20, their return for the period January 1 to June 20 must be filed by April 16.
The final return can also serve as a claim for a tax refund if there was an overpayment.
In such cases, Form 1310 must be completed and attached to the return.
Extensions of time to file are available under unusual circumstances.
Taxpayers must apply by filing Form 2688 or submitting a written request to the District Director of Internal Revenue.
The application must include reasons for the extension, whether previous returns were filed on time, and whether estimated tax payments were made.
Extensions are not granted automatically and require substantial justification.
U.S. citizens abroad on the due date may be granted an automatic extension until June 15.
Military and naval personnel stationed outside the U.S. or in Alaska are also eligible for this extension.
A statement must be attached to the return to confirm the taxpayer's location on the due date.
If taxes are not paid by the due date, interest at a rate of 6% per year must be paid.
This applies even if an extension was granted for filing.
If a taxpayer owes less than $1 in additional tax, the amount is forgiven.
Taxpayers who file Form 1040 or 1040A and owe additional tax should remit the payment with their return unless the amount is less than $1.
The IRS allows taxpayers to correct errors or request extensions, but all deadlines and requirements must be met to avoid penalties and interest.
stem: According to the passage, which of the following statements is true?

options.B: U.S. citizens abroad must submit a statement to the IRS to qualify for the automatic extension.
options.C: Taxpayers who file for the first time can automatically receive an extension of time to file without providing any justification.
options.D: Nonresident aliens in Canada or Mexico who are subject to tax withholding follow a tax filing schedule similar to U.S. citizens, but with a one-day delay.

passage: Mike sat in deep thought, trying to understand the meaning of the word 'church' that kept coming up in Jubal's conversations.

He struggled to find a Martian equivalent, something that could hold the same meaning in a different language and culture.
The word 'God' also troubled him, as it did not have a direct translation in Martian.
He repeated the phrase 'Thou art God' to himself, trying to feel its truth, but it never quite fit.
He could speak the English sentence and the Martian word at the same time, and this helped him feel closer to understanding.
The more he practiced, the more he felt a shift in his perception, like a door opening just a crack.
By midnight, he felt lighter, clearer, and more awake than he had in days.
He wanted to share his new understanding with others, especially Mahmoud, but he had already left.
So Mike went out to find someone else—perhaps a water brother.
He was lucky enough to meet one, and they greeted each other with warmth and happiness.
Mike felt a strong need for company, a sense of connection that had been missing before.
They went to get something to eat, and Mike was pleased to find that his water brother also felt hungry.
As they sat outside in the warm night, Mike thought about the beauty of the world around him and the people in it.
He could see clearly in the dark, a skill he had learned from his Martian upbringing and his human teachers.
He was learning to be considerate of others' weaknesses, like their sensitivity to cold.
He imagined the snow, each flake a unique crystal, and he wanted to feel it with his own hands.
For now, he was content with the warm night and the company of a friend.
The lights under the water glowed softly, and Mike felt a sense of peace and purpose growing inside him.

Brain ships, like the one Helva would control, were no longer experimental.

She also studied logistics, mental hygiene, and space law, all of which were essential for her future role.
While she was studying, she was also being conditioned without realizing it.

Helva's civilization had groups that worried about the ethics of shell people, but most objections were quieted when they saw how the bodies were hidden.

passage: In the heart of New Orleans, a crowd gathered in Congo Square to watch a lively calinda dance.
The event was part of a long tradition among enslaved people from Haiti and Louisiana.
A young woman with striking green eyes stood apart from the others, watching the dancers with quiet intensity.
She held a small ginger cake and chewed it slowly, her gaze fixed on a man who danced with a king snake around his neck.
The dancer moved with confidence and strength, drawing admiration from the onlookers.
His bronze skin and well-defined features marked him as someone with European ancestry in his background.
The woman, dressed in fine clothes, turned to a tall man beside her and whispered, 'Look at your watch, Col. Garvier.
The calinda is about to begin.'
Colonel Henri Garvier was a respected slave owner known for his progressive views.
He chuckled and gave the signal for the dance to start.
The enslaved people rushed to the center, forming a circle around a young drummer named Johnny No-Name.
Johnny hit two bleached steer bones against a gourd, creating a rhythmic beat that filled the air.
He wore brass earrings that jingled as he danced, his body trembling with excitement.
The dancers moved in a sensual, hypnotic way, a style passed down from generations of enslaved people.
Among the onlookers was Delphine Lalaurie, a woman of high society and a powerful figure in New Orleans.
She sipped lemonade from a silver cup, her beauty and poise making her stand out.
A man in blue livery stood nearby, his dark skin and sharp features suggesting he was once a slave but now lived as a servant in her household.
He was proud of his position and imitated the manners of the white elite.
Delphine had a reputation for being fashionable and generous, but she also had a cruel side that would soon be revealed.
She gestured toward the dancer with the snake, a young man named Dandy Brandon.
He was known for his charm and magnetism, though he was shy and inexperienced with women.
Delphine approached him with a mix of curiosity and control, asking his name and testing his strength.
She examined him closely, her touch firm and commanding.
After a few moments, she signaled to her driver, a man named Aristide, and handed him a bag of gold coins.
'Find Master Prieur and give him this money for the boy,' she said.

passage: The man was overwhelmed by the endless details of daily life, which left little time for the things he truly wanted to do.
Each day seemed to bring new tasks that demanded immediate attention, making life feel like a constant state of preparation.
He dreamed of a future where he could finally read, garden, or walk through the woods with his dogs in the late afternoon.
Yet, his dogs had become a distant memory, once a joyful part of his life but now absent from his plans.
He had almost forgotten them, even though they had once romped around him on walks, yelping with delight and returning with muddy paws.
Dogs had a way of boosting one's ego, constantly reminding you that you were important.
Even if they noticed your flaws, they would never let it affect their affection.
Now, however, it was increasingly clear that there would be no dogs in his future.
He couldn't take them into the city apartment when he traveled for work, and leaving them behind for days would only confuse and distress them.
He often wondered why he couldn't live in one place like everyone else, but this restlessness had always defined him.
He worried about his inability to complete simple tasks, often waking in the night to fret over it.
In the past, he had managed to build a business, raise a family, and serve on numerous committees while still finding time for evenings out or work at home.
He questioned whether time itself changed with age, speeding up as if the universe were skipping through the final chapter.
Or was it simply that older people worked more slowly, taking longer to write letters, shave, or clean a barn?
Perhaps they became perfectionists, endlessly polishing and reluctant to let go.
Some people, he thought, were born with a compulsion to complicate their lives, while others could remain motionless and content, like lizards in the sun, too indolent to blink.
He suspected he belonged to the first group, unconsciously building pressure in a world that demanded none.
Maybe the reason he couldn't find time for reading, roaming, or gardening was because he didn't truly want to do them.
There was no compulsion behind them, no one waiting for him to act.
Throughout his life, he had only done what was necessary, and now it was difficult to do anything for its own sake.
He looked at his watch, which showed five minutes after four.
On a distant farm, a rooster crowed, and an associate answered from the valley below.
He turned over impatiently, pulling the sheet over his head against the treacherous encroachment of dawn.
At least he could take one small step forward.
He decided to buy the equipment for his workshop.
Thus committed, he went to the hardware store and purchased a full set of tools, including a power saw and other gadgets he didn't yet know how to use.

passage: Marty stood on the red-clay road, facing a man with a graying beard and piercing, red-threaded eyes.

He asked if any of them could give him a ride back to Jarrodsville, offering to pay for the favor.

They piled into the waiting cars, engines roared to life, and the vehicles sped off in different directions.
One station wagon and an old Plymouth headed east toward Jarrodsville, leaving tire tracks in the mud.
A Ford and a pickup truck vanished west toward Sanford's Run, their engines growling as they disappeared.
In seconds, the road was empty again, the only sound being the distant rumble of thunder.
Marty stood alone as storm clouds gathered ominously in the sky, the air thick with tension.
Thunder rumbled in the distance, breaking the silence and echoing across the quiet countryside.
He looked back at the house, thinking he saw a pale face at a window, perhaps Dora May watching silently.
He glanced at the nearby farmhouses, but no one came out, the homes dark and still.
Telephone poles lined the road, tall and mocking, their wires stretching out into the distant horizon.
Not a single wire reached into the silent homes beside the road, cutting them off from the world.
Marty had no choice but to walk, the rain already turning the dirt road into a deep, muddy quagmire.
Jarrodsville was more than three miles away, the journey ahead long and treacherous in the worsening weather.
He faced east and began walking down the left side of the road, his boots sinking into the mud with each step.
After a few steps, he paused and rolled up the cuffs of his already damp and mud-caked trousers.

passage: Marty Land saw a man with a graying beard and red-veined eyes.
The man chewed gum and exuded the smell of whiskey.
He regarded Marty steadily and unblinkingly.
Marty recognized him as Acey Squire, the proprietor of a juke joint.
Marty smiled at Squire and asked if anyone had seen the cab that had been waiting for him.
No one answered, so he suggested that someone might be willing to drive him back to Jarrodsville for a fee.
The seventeen men stood in silence, their faces expressionless, as they stared at Marty.
Then, to his complete surprise, they all moved at the same time.
As if a silent signal had been given, they piled into the waiting cars.
The engines roared to life, and within moments, the vehicles were speeding in opposite directions.
One car headed east toward Jarrodsville, while another sped west toward Sanford’s Run.
In seconds, all four cars vanished from sight, leaving Marty standing alone on the red-clay road.
Storm clouds gathered ominously in the sky, and from a great distance, thunder rumbled and broke the silence.
Marty looked back toward the dilapidated house and thought he saw a pale face at a window.
Perhaps it was Dora May.
Perhaps she was glad that they hadn’t hurt him.
He noticed other farmhouses nearby, no more than a hundred yards away.
One stood across the road, while another was a little further down.
There were many more between there and Jarrodsville.
Telephone poles lined the road, their tall frames and wires stretching out into the distance like silent sentinels.
Yet not a single wire reached into the silent, isolated houses that stood along the red-clay road.
Marty realized he had no choice but to walk, as Jarrodsville was more than three miles away along a muddy dirt road.
The rain had turned the path into a quagmire, and he faced east, beginning to walk slowly down the left side of the road.
After a few steps, he paused and turned up the cuffs of his trousers, which were already damp and caked with mud.
The quiet road stretched ahead of him, and he walked on alone, the only sound the soft crunch of his boots in the wet earth.
The storm clouds continued to gather, and the distant rumble of thunder reminded him of the isolation and danger he now faced.
Marty felt the weight of the situation as he moved forward, unsure of what awaited him in Jarrodsville.
The red-clay road seemed endless, and the houses along the way stood like forgotten sentinels in the gathering gloom.
He kept walking, his mind turning over the events that had just unfolded and the strange behavior of the men who had disappeared.
Marty Land walked on, the wind beginning to pick up as the storm drew closer and the rain threatened to fall at any moment.

passage: The Central Valley in California is one of the world's most productive agricultural regions.
In 1960, it became the center of a major labor dispute between the Agricultural Workers Organizing Committee (AWOC) and local growers.
The Department of Employment found itself in the middle of this conflict due to its role in the farm labor placement program.
It tried to remain neutral but often had to make decisions that upset one side or the other.
Some publications accused the department of favoring growers, while others claimed it supported the union.
Despite these criticisms, the department believed its actions were necessary and fair.
For years, attempts to organize farm workers in California had failed due to a lack of funding, leadership, and support.
However, in 1960, the situation changed.
The AFL-CIO provided financial and organizational support to the AWOC, and experienced leaders helped guide the effort.
This support made the union's actions more effective, especially in negotiating better wages.
The AWOC used strikes and picket lines strategically, focusing on specific crops and areas at key times.
The Department of Employment became involved in these disputes because of its responsibilities under the Wagner-Peyser Act.
This federal law governs the referral of workers to jobs, especially during labor disputes.
Under the law, the department must give workers notice of strikes or lockouts before referring them to a job.
The Wagner-Peyser Act also gives the Secretary of Labor the authority to create regulations to carry out the law.
One such regulation prohibits referrals to jobs that are vacant due to a strike or are part of an ongoing labor dispute.
However, the regulation allows referrals in some cases if workers are given written notice of the dispute.
For example, if only part of a farm is affected by a strike, workers can still be referred to unaffected areas.
A specific case in Yuba County tested this regulation.
The AWOC called a strike at a pear orchard, and the Department of Employment stopped referring workers to the employer.
The grower challenged this decision in court, and the court ordered the department to resume referrals.
The Attorney General of California then moved the case to federal court, arguing that the issue involved federal jurisdiction.
The situation highlighted the complexity of labor laws and the challenges of balancing the rights of workers and employers.
The Department of Employment continued to face difficult decisions as the labor dispute evolved.
Its role in managing referrals during strikes became a key part of the broader labor-management conflict.
The outcome of the court case would influence how the Wagner-Peyser Act was applied in future disputes.
The events of 1960 marked a turning point in the struggle for farm workers' rights in California.
The support from the AFL-CIO and the strategic actions of the AWOC changed the dynamics of labor relations in the agricultural sector.
The legal and political battles that followed set the stage for future labor reforms and shaped the labor landscape in California.

passage: President John F. Kennedy faced a difficult decision in early 1961 about whether to meet with Soviet Premier Nikita Khrushchev.
At first, he was not eager to hold a summit, believing that real progress in Cold War diplomacy required more than just a meeting.
He felt that military, economic, and ideological power were the key factors in dealing with the Soviet Union.
However, as tensions between the U.S. and the Soviet Union worsened, Kennedy reconsidered.
The situation in East-West relations had become increasingly unstable, and this change in the international climate influenced his thinking.
By June, the White House officially announced that Kennedy would meet Khrushchev in Vienna on June 3 and 4.
The meeting was not intended for formal negotiations, but it was seen as a crucial step in preventing a potential crisis.
Despite efforts to downplay its importance, many believed it would be one of the most significant Cold War encounters.
The history of U.S.-Soviet summits had been mixed.
In 1955, a Geneva summit created a false sense of progress, while in 1959, the Camp David meeting failed to resolve key issues.
In 1960, Khrushchev's angry response to the U-2 incident destroyed a planned summit in Paris.
These past experiences made Kennedy cautious.
He did not want to appear weak or desperate to meet Khrushchev.
However, he also recognized the need to engage with the Soviet leader.
Kennedy believed that a personal meeting could help clarify intentions and prevent misunderstandings.
He was especially concerned about the stalled nuclear test ban talks in Geneva, where the Soviet Union had demanded a three-way control system that the U.S. rejected.
Kennedy feared that a breakdown in these talks could lead to more nuclear weapons spreading to other countries.
In addition, events in Cuba and Laos had further strained relations.
The U.S. had failed to stop the Cuban Revolution, and the situation in Laos suggested a lack of Western resolve.
These incidents made Kennedy worry that Khrushchev might misjudge the West’s strength.
As a result, he saw the need for a direct conversation.
The meeting in Vienna was not expected to solve all problems, but it was a necessary step in Cold War diplomacy.
Kennedy hoped it would help prevent catastrophe and show the world that the U.S. was willing to work toward peace.
The outcome of the meeting would be closely watched by people around the world.

options.B: The meeting was expected to produce a binding international treaty.
options.C: Kennedy was responsible for the spread of nuclear weapons to other countries.
options.D: Kennedy thought a face-to-face meeting could help avoid dangerous misjudgments between the U.S. and the Soviet Union.

passage: Seeds play a major role in many industrial applications around the world.
Oil from certain seeds is used to make paints and varnishes that protect and beautify surfaces.
Flax and tung seeds, for example, produce drying oils that form hard, smooth films when they dry.
These oils are essential in creating resinlike substances used in wood and metal finishes.
Artists also use drying oils to carry pigments and preserve their paintings for many years.
Some oils, like those from poppy seeds, are especially valued for their quality and durability.
Other seeds, such as soybean, cotton, and corn, produce semidrying oils used in a variety of industrial products.
These oils are mixed with drying oils to improve their performance in coatings and finishes.
In addition to paints, seed oils are used in the production of soaps, detergents, and plastics.
Castor oil, once used as a medicine, is now in high demand as a lubricant and a key ingredient in hydraulic fluids and chemical manufacturing.
Almond oil, another type of oil, is used in cosmetics and perfumes, although it is now less common due to its scarcity and the risk of being mixed with other oils.
Solid fats from seeds like mahua, shea, and coconut are used to make candles in tropical regions.
Starch from seeds is also important for industry, especially in the paper, textile, and food-processing sectors.
Corn and wheat are the main sources of starch in countries like the United States, Canada, and Australia.
In other parts of the world, starchy roots and tubers are processed for starch when grains are not the main crop.
Gums extracted from seeds have many uses as well.
Guar gum, locust bean gum, and psyllium are used as thickeners, stabilizers, and dispersing agents in food, drugs, and paper production.
Guar gum helps make salad dressings smooth and keeps ice cream from melting too quickly.
Quince seed gum is used in beauty products like wave-setting lotions.
Psyllium was once considered a nuisance but is now used in laxatives and dietary supplements.
Locust bean gum is also important in the paper industry to break up fiber lumps.
Overall, seeds contribute significantly to both food and nonfood industries, providing essential materials for everyday products.

options.B: Drying oils are used only to enhance the appearance of surfaces and not for protection.
options.C: Guar gum is used to improve the texture of food products.
options.D: Castor oil is no longer a major component in modern industrial applications due to the availability of synthetic alternatives.

passage: The early 1900s marked a major turning point in the study of early English history, as new methods and tools began to shape modern scholarship.
During this time, archaeology became a more scientific and reliable tool for historians, moving beyond its earlier status as an antiquarian pastime.
Scholars like Frederick Haverfield and Reginald Smith helped raise the standards of archaeological research through their work on the Victoria County Histories.
E.T.
Leeds' 'Archaeology Of The Anglo-Saxon Settlements' provided a clear and organized summary of the archaeological evidence available at the time.
This change in archaeology also affected the study of place-names, which had long been used to understand early English history.
However, without a strong knowledge of Germanic languages, these studies often led to confusion and error.
It was not until the early 20th century that place-name studies became more scientific, thanks to the work of scholars like J.H.
Round and W.H.
Stevenson.
Diplomatic studies also improved, with new editorial standards for historical documents that built upon the achievements of 19th-century scholars.
These changes in methods and tools helped create the modern techniques used in early English scholarship today.
The improvements in archaeology and place-name studies were especially important for understanding the Saxon Shore and its historical context.
These new methods led to a reevaluation of older theories, especially those from the Oxford school of scholars like Stubbs, Freeman, and Green.
They had believed the Anglo-Saxon conquest of Britain was a sudden and complete event, but new evidence and critical thinking challenged this view.
Charles Plummer, for example, questioned the accuracy of these traditional accounts in his edition of Bede, voicing early doubts about the 'elaborate superstructure' built over slim foundations.
Other scholars, like Sir Henry Howorth and W.H.
Stevenson, also criticized the reliability of the West Saxon annals and the writings of Guest.

By the early 1900s, many historians were more skeptical of the traditional narratives, with Ferdinand Lot, a French scholar, writing in 1913 that it was hard to believe the old stories of the Saxon conquest.
However, modern scholars did not fully reject the old sources, instead taking a balanced approach, using the old texts carefully and in combination with other evidence.
Most now agree that while Bede, Gildas, and the Anglo-Saxon Chronicles are not completely reliable, they still provide a rough outline of the English settlement of southern Britain.
Despite these changes, the idea of a sudden and massive invasion by the Anglo-Saxons remained popular for many years, with some scholars even suggesting such an invasion happened around 450 AD.

However, new theories, like Frederick Seebohm's idea of continuity between Roman and Anglo-Saxon times, challenged this view by suggesting that Anglo-Saxon society developed gradually, not through a sudden invasion.
Scholars like F.W.
Maitland and Sir Paul Vinogradoff opposed Seebohm's ideas, but his work still influenced some historians, including H.L.
Gray and Zachrisson.

passage: The early 1900s marked a major turning point in the study of early English history, as new methods and tools began to shape modern scholarship.
During this time, archaeology became a more scientific and reliable tool for historians, moving beyond its earlier status as an antiquarian pastime.
Scholars like Frederick Haverfield and Reginald Smith helped raise the standards of archaeological research through their work on the Victoria County Histories.
E.T.
Leeds' 'Archaeology Of The Anglo-Saxon Settlements' provided a clear and organized summary of the archaeological evidence available at the time.
This change in archaeology also affected the study of place-names, which had long been used to understand early English history.
However, without a strong knowledge of Germanic languages, these studies often led to confusion and error.
It was not until the early 20th century that place-name studies became more scientific, thanks to the work of scholars like J.H.
Round and W.H.
Stevenson.
Diplomatic studies also improved, with new editorial standards for historical documents that built upon the achievements of 19th-century scholars.
These changes in methods and tools helped create the modern techniques used in early English scholarship today.
The improvements in archaeology and place-name studies were especially important for understanding the Saxon Shore and its historical context.
These new methods led to a reevaluation of older theories, especially those from the Oxford school of scholars like Stubbs, Freeman, and Green.
They had believed the Anglo-Saxon conquest of Britain was a sudden and complete event, but new evidence and critical thinking challenged this view.
Charles Plummer, for example, questioned the accuracy of these traditional accounts in his edition of Bede, voicing early doubts about the 'elaborate superstructure' built over slim foundations.
Other scholars, like Sir Henry Howorth and W.H.
Stevenson, also criticized the reliability of the West Saxon annals and the writings of Guest.

By the early 1900s, many historians were more skeptical of the traditional narratives, with Ferdinand Lot, a French scholar, writing in 1913 that it was hard to believe the old stories of the Saxon conquest.
However, modern scholars did not fully reject the old sources, instead taking a balanced approach, using the old texts carefully and in combination with other evidence.
Most now agree that while Bede, Gildas, and the Anglo-Saxon Chronicles are not completely reliable, they still provide a rough outline of the English settlement of southern Britain.
Despite these changes, the idea of a sudden and massive invasion by the Anglo-Saxons remained popular for many years, with some scholars even suggesting such an invasion happened around 450 AD.

However, new theories, like Frederick Seebohm's idea of continuity between Roman and Anglo-Saxon times, challenged this view by suggesting that Anglo-Saxon society developed gradually, not through a sudden invasion.
Scholars like F.W.
Maitland and Sir Paul Vinogradoff opposed Seebohm's ideas, but his work still influenced some historians, including H.L.
Gray and Zachrisson.

Today, the debate continues, with some supporting the idea of continuity and others believing in a more dramatic change, though most scholars now look for a more balanced and nuanced understanding of early English history.
stem: According to the passage, which of the following statements is true?

options.B: Modern scholars use traditional texts such as Bede and the Anglo-Saxon Chronicles alongside archaeological and other evidence to develop a more nuanced and balanced understanding of early English history.
options.C: By the early 1900s, most historians had fully accepted the theory of a gradual development of Anglo-Saxon society without a major invasion.
options.D: The Oxford school of scholars, including Stubbs and Freeman, were the first to make place-name studies more scientific.

In the same year, Governor Notte also proclaimed Armed Forces Day on May 20 to honor the service and sacrifice of military members.
He explained that 1961 marked the 14th anniversary of the unification of the U.S. Armed Forces under the National Security Act of 1947.
The governor emphasized that national defense is a shared responsibility and a major investment in peace and freedom.

Through these proclamations, Governor Notte aimed to inspire pride and unity among the people of Rhode Island.
He believed that remembering the past and honoring those who serve were essential to building a better future for the state and the nation.

passage: Avant-garde choreographers often focus on pure movement, using minimal costumes and simple sets to highlight the dancer's form.
Robert Rauschenberg, a neo-dadaist artist, collaborated with many of these choreographers, creating costumes and backdrops that blend with the performers.
For Merce Cunningham's 'Summerspace,' he designed white costumes with points of color, making dancers and background appear as one.
For Taylor's 'Images And Reflections,' he created diaphanous tents that reveal and conceal the performer, and a cape lined with grass.
Nikolais, another choreographer, experimented with masks, objects, and lights to depersonalize the dancer and create a new theatrical being.
He used hoops, poles, and capes as extensions of the body, helping the performer lose their sense of self.
The interplay of light and costume could transform the dancer into a 'finial,' a decorative object.
In these performances, props and costumes become animized, merging with the dancer to form a unified entity.
This approach allows for new movement ideas that treat dancer and object as a single unit.
Avant-garde choreographers have thus expanded the materials available for dance composition.
However, without narrative or emotional continuity, they must find new ways to unify their diverse elements.
Some draw from other art forms, applying methods used in poetry, painting, and music to their work.
An approach inspired by Charles Olson's projective verse suggests that one perception should lead directly to another.
Choreographers trust their intuition, allowing movement to evolve naturally from one idea to the next.
They reject conventional structures, instead following the internal logic of their experience.
This method mirrors the work of abstract expressionist painters, who value the essence of their experience over rigid forms.
Surrealism, an earlier art movement, also influenced choreographers by suggesting that dream-like associations can link disparate elements in a meaningful way.
Contemporary painters often focus on the essence of their subject rather than its physical form, using abstraction to capture deeper truths.
Similarly, choreographers may prioritize the process of creation over the final product.
Katherine Litz noted that 'the becoming, the process of realization, is the dance.'
This means that the choreographer must feel the rightness of each movement as it follows the previous one.
The sequence can involve sharp contrasts, such as a meditative sway followed by a sudden leap.
Or it can involve subtle shifts in rhythm, size, or emphasis.
These techniques allow choreographers to maintain continuity while exploring new forms of movement and expression.

options.D: Avant-garde choreographers give more importance to the end result more than how the work develops.

passage: Wilson arrived in Annisberg, a town in Alabama, and visited the Allen African Methodist Episcopal Church.

This group of worshippers, mostly older women, played a central role in the Sunday services.
Their participation was intense and emotional, often reaching a state of hysteria.
The service began with a quiet, conversational tone and gradually built up to loud, passionate appeals to God.
The Amen corner then took over, creating a powerful and dramatic atmosphere.
They shouted, danced, wept, and sometimes even seemed to be in a trance.
This form of worship had deep roots, tracing back to African traditions and the influence of the Greek chorus.
Many people in the congregation found the experience deeply moving and meaningful.
Visitors, especially white people, often watched from a distance, sometimes with amusement or confusion.
Wilson, the new pastor, was unprepared for the intensity of the scene.
He had delivered a calm and direct sermon, but as soon as he mentioned the name of the previous pastor, the Amen corner erupted.

After the service, people left in silence, and Wilson felt uncertain about how he was perceived.
In the weeks that followed, he explored the town and the church further.
He found the church building in a terrible state, with no proper plumbing or sanitation.
The pastor’s salary was far below what he considered acceptable.
Wilson also noticed the poor conditions in the Black Bottom, a neglected area where many lived in poverty and disease.
He was determined to bring change, but he knew it would not be easy.
The community had its own traditions, its own way of life, and it was not ready to let go of them.
Wilson realized that his role would not just be to preach but to understand and connect with a people who had lived through years of hardship and loss.
The Amen corner was not just a part of the service; it was a symbol of their strength, their pain, and their faith.
He would need to learn from them as much as they would from him.

passage: The Essex Merrimack Bridge in Massachusetts is a historically significant structure that was built in the late 1700s.
It was the first covered bridge in the United States and is notable for its innovative design and construction.
The idea for the bridge was first proposed in 1791 by a group of citizens from Newburyport, who petitioned the General Court for permission to build it.
The petition explained that the bridge would provide a safe and reliable connection between Newburyport and Salisbury, especially during all seasons and tides.
After much discussion and some opposition, the court granted a charter for the project in January 1792.
The bridge was completed and opened on November 26 of that same year.
Timothy Palmer, a local inventor, was responsible for the design and supervision of the bridge, even though he had no prior experience in bridge building.
The structure was made of wood and featured a large arch spanning 160 feet.
It was described in detail by Rev.
Timothy Dwight in his 1821 book, where he praised the bridge's appearance and engineering.
Initially, the bridge was not covered, but by 1810, the northern section was likely roofed for protection.
A famous engraving from 1793 shows the bridge in its original form, using more than 6,000 tons of timber.
The bridge was celebrated with a public dinner on July 4, 1793, held in a tavern built by the bridge company on Deer Island.
One of the early shareholders, Timothy Dexter, gave a speech at the event, which was said to be eloquent, though it may have been in French or heavily influenced by the festivities.
The southern part of the bridge was later replaced in 1810 with a chain suspension bridge, designed by James Finley and built by John Templeman.
Timothy Palmer oversaw this new construction and even advertised his services as an expert in chain bridge technology.
Unfortunately, the chain bridge was not as durable as the original wooden structure.
It collapsed in 1827, taking a horse, wagon, two men, and four oxen with it.
Although the horse and men survived, the oxen drowned in the river.
Despite this disaster, the bridge was rebuilt and reopened in 1827.
The original wooden bridge on the Salisbury side remained standing until 1882, when it was eventually removed.
Today, the Essex Merrimack Bridge is remembered as an important milestone in American engineering and a symbol of early innovation in bridge construction.

passage: Soybean seeds are among the most important legumes in the world, especially in the United States, where half of the global crop is grown.

In Asian countries, soybeans are transformed into a wide range of traditional and modern food products.
American scientists have developed new methods to improve the use of soybeans in foods like tofu, miso, and tempeh.
Soybean products such as flour, grits, flakes, milk, and curd are also available in the U.S. market.
Peanuts are the second most important legume, mainly used for their oil.
However, in the U.S., people often consume the entire peanut, especially when it is blanched and roasted for peanut butter or snacks.
Cereal grains, when combined with legumes like soybeans or peas, form a large part of the diet in many parts of Asia and Africa.
In contrast, people in Western Europe and North America rely less on grains and more on meat, dairy, and processed foods.
In countries like Australia, New Zealand, and Argentina, where large areas of land are used for grazing, meat consumption is high, and seeds play a smaller role in the diet.
Livestock feed accounts for a significant portion of the world’s cereal crop, with much of it going to swine, dairy cows, and poultry.
In the U.S., about 90 percent of corn is used for animal feed, with the rest going to human food and industrial products.
Other seeds, such as sorghum and barley, are also processed for livestock feed, along with byproducts from oilseed crushing.
Industrial use of seeds is growing, with oil-bearing seeds like flax, castor, and tung playing key roles in manufacturing.
The oils from these seeds are used in paints, varnishes, and protective coatings for wood and metal.
Artists also use drying oils, such as those from poppy seeds, to carry pigments and preserve their work.
Nondrying oils like castor oil are now in high demand as lubricants and for use in hydraulic systems.
Almond oil, once popular in perfumes, is still used in cosmetics and pharmaceuticals.
Industrial oils are also important in the production of soaps, detergents, and plastics.
Solid fats from seeds like mahua, shea, and coconut are used to make candles in tropical regions.
Seeds are a major source of starch, especially in countries where corn and wheat are widely grown.
In other parts of the world, starchy tubers and roots are processed for industrial use.
Starch is essential in the paper, textile, and food industries.
Gums extracted from seeds like guar, locust bean, and psyllium are used in food, medicine, and paper production.

passage: In construction, a key strategy is to build from the inside out rather than from the outside in.
This method avoids unnecessary delays and costly mistakes by positioning components before enclosing them.
For example, wall cabinets and appliances should be installed before walls are built, as this ensures a proper fit and reduces the need for adjustments.
Similarly, bathtubs should be placed before the bathroom is enclosed, as moving heavy fixtures through narrow spaces can be difficult and time-consuming.
Plumbing and heating systems must also be completed before walls are closed in, as it is far easier to make repairs and connections in an open space.
In conventional construction, windows should be installed before framing around them, which reduces the need for shimming and saves time.
Disappearing stairs to an attic and overhead ducts should be installed before drywall is added to the ceiling.
Builders like Bob Schmitt prefer to erect the final wall between the house and garage last, allowing materials to be delivered indoors and unloaded under shelter.
This approach mirrors the efficiency seen in the automotive and trailer industries, where components are assembled in a logical sequence to maximize productivity.
The revolution in materials handling has transformed the construction industry by enabling the use of larger, prefabricated components.
This shift reduces on-site labor and increases the use of shop fabrication, where items can be made more precisely and at lower costs.
Materials handling is now more efficient than in 1929, and it has changed when and how tasks are performed on-site.
For instance, driveways can now be installed early in the process, rather than at the end.
Builder-dealer relationships have also evolved, with many builders now partnering with dealers who can deliver materials directly to the work site.
This teamwork reduces costs and improves efficiency by ensuring that materials arrive in the right place at the right time.
Clarence Thompson, a leader in the industry, emphasizes that dealers must justify their mark-up by providing services that save the builder money.
The revolution in materials handling has made this possible.
Despite progress, challenges remain.
Five years ago, only a small percentage of lumber dealers were equipped to handle unit loads, and even fewer builders were ready to receive them.
Today, most lumber dealers serving the new-house market are mechanized, and nearly all can deliver materials in a way that lowers costs for the builder.
The industry now recognizes the importance of collaboration between manufacturers, carriers, equipment makers, dealers, and builders.
This teamwork is essential for reducing the costs of materials handling, which can account for up to a quarter of total construction expenses.
The revolution is still in progress, but it has already made a significant impact on how homes are built and how materials are delivered.

passage: Scientists study the magnetic properties of a compound called Af, which has three unpaired electrons on its chromium atoms.
The crystal structure of Af is simple, and the position of hydrogen atoms in the strong Af bond is of particular interest.
The hydrogen bond in Af is thought to be symmetric when the bond length is around 2.4 to 2.5 angstroms.
X-ray studies by Douglass show that Af has a trigonal structure with a space group that requires the hydrogen bond to be symmetric.
However, the exact symmetry of the bond remains uncertain due to the complexity of the crystal structure.
The structure of Af consists of layers of chromium atoms between two layers of oxygen atoms.
These oxygen layers are close-packed, and each chromium atom is surrounded by a distorted octahedron of oxygen atoms.
The layers are joined by hydrogen bonds and stacked in a repeating pattern every three layers.
The hydrogen atoms may be positioned in one of three ways: symmetrically between the oxygen layers, asymmetrically but randomly, or asymmetrically in an ordered pattern.
The first possibility is considered unlikely due to the absence of a piezoelectric effect and the general chemical structure.
The second possibility is more likely because the hydrogen atoms are well separated and do not influence each other.
The third possibility would require a larger unit cell, which has not been observed.
Therefore, the main question is whether the hydrogen atoms are symmetrically or asymmetrically placed.
The crystal structure of Af is unique among similar compounds, and the bond angles and distances are within expected limits.
The volume per oxygen atom is about normal, but the oxygen atoms may not be geometrically equivalent if the crystal lacks a center of symmetry.
This lack of symmetry could allow the hydrogen atoms to occupy general positions along the (111) axis.
The study of Af is important because it helps scientists understand how electron paramagnetic effects influence nuclear resonance.
The electron effects can be separated from nuclear effects, providing valuable information about the structure and motion of atoms.
The paramagnetic dipole effects give insights into particle shapes, while the nuclear dipole effects relate to the motion of hydrogen nuclei.
The symmetry of the Af bond has implications for the overall structure and stability of the compound.
Further research is needed to confirm the exact position of the hydrogen atoms and the nature of the hydrogen bond in Af.

options.A: The hydrogen bond in Af is not confirmed to be symmetric, despite initial suggestions from X-ray studies.
options.B: The nuclear dipole effects are the primary source of information about the positions of hydrogen atoms in Af, as they are the only effects that can detect the motion of hydrogen nuclei.
options.C: The crystal structure of Af has been completely determined, and the hydrogen atom positions are now well established.
options.D: The hydrogen atoms in Af are likely in an ordered, asymmetric pattern because the crystal structure shows no signs of a larger unit cell.

passage: Martin's life had become dominated by a pair of white cotton shorts.

He remembered when he first saw her at a party, standing across the room with her dark hair curling around her neck like petals.
He thought of touching it, of running his fingers through it, searching for a sign of veining that might reveal its true shade under the darkness.
So he sought her out, spoke to her, and thought of his hand in her hair or against her back, pressed on the column of vertebrae that held her so magnificently straight and unyielding.
They married quickly, and at first, life felt exciting and full of promise.
On the tenth day after the wedding, Martin left the shorts on the floor and told Dolores he wouldn’t pick them up.
The next morning, the shorts were still there, and he smiled to himself, thinking she would take care of it.
But when he came home, the shorts were still on the floor, and the rest of the room had been groomed to a superhuman neatness.
The disheveled shorts gave the room a strange note of incongruity, like a mole on a beautiful face.
Martin realized Dolores was waiting for him to act, thinking he would get nervous as the guests arrived.
Quietly, he determined to foil her by being just as stubborn as she was, believing his nerves were as strong as hers.
She would rush to the bedroom when the doorbell rang, but he was prepared to outlast her.
The doorbell rang ten minutes early, and Martin stood near the front door, looking toward the bedroom fifteen feet away.
He had no intention of moving the shorts, and he was ready for whatever Dolores would do next.
The tension in the room was palpable, with the shorts lying defiantly in the center of the carpet.
Martin’s mind was focused, and he was determined to see how far this small battle over the shorts would go.

The construction of Hotei requires about 400 hours of work and uses one-inch mahogany wood.
The wood is cut into planks and shaped for parts like battens and frames.
Builders use special silicon bronze nails and a strong glue made of resorcinol.
First, they lay out the six frames and the transom on a level floor, marking each in different colors to avoid mistakes.
The transom is built first, with joints glued and nailed together.
A half-inch plywood panel is then attached to the transom for added strength.
Frames are connected using 3/8-inch plywood gussets and the same type of nails.
These frames are notched for the keelson and chines but not for the battens, which helps keep the structure strong.
A jig is built to hold the frames in place during construction, making sure everything stays lined up.
Once the frames are set, a three-inch-wide piece of mahogany is placed between the first two frames.
The frames are glued and fastened to this piece, and small blocks are added for extra support.
Over this, the laminated front part and keelson are joined together.
The keelson is made of two three-inch-wide pieces and is installed next, forming a strong central backbone of the boat.

After 25,000 deaths, the 50 state highway commissioners should be arrested.
They would be executed, in a public ceremony on July 4, 1963, at the geographic center of the U.S. population.
This symbolic act would highlight the government's responsibility for the lives of its citizens.
The event, would include dignitaries from new African nations and be accompanied by music.
The author believes that this shocking action would challenge the belief that constant movement is the goal of life.
He argues that staying in one place can be valuable, though this idea is now seen as outdated.
The proposal is meant to provoke thought and change behavior.
The author acknowledges that appeals to morality and reason have not worked, so a strong deterrent is needed.
He believes that making officials accountable for excessive deaths could reduce the number of accidents.

The event would also have a social impact by challenging harmful beliefs about constant movement.
While the idea is extreme, the author believes it is necessary to address a serious problem.
The goal is to make people rethink their relationship with cars and the value of human life.

passage: In ancient India, a tribe imagined the Earth resting on the backs of elephants, which stood on a giant tortoise.
This idea, while incorrect, reflects an early attempt to explain the unknown using what was familiar.
Today, cosmologists study the universe using physics, mathematics, and astronomy to solve cosmic mysteries.
In 1959, the BBC hosted a series of talks by four scientists, including Dr. Bonnor, Professor Bondi, Dr. Lyttleton, and Dr. Whitrow, who discussed different theories of the universe.
Dr. Bonnor argued that the universe is expanding and will eventually contract, creating a cycle of expansion and collapse.
He explained that galaxies are moving away from each other at high speeds and that this expansion has been ongoing for billions of years.
According to Dr. Bonnor, the universe will one day begin to contract, and galaxies will move toward a common center.
After many more billions of years, the contraction will slow and reverse again, leading to a new cycle of expansion.
Professor Bondi, however, supported the steady-state theory, which claims that matter is continuously created in space to maintain a constant density.
He argued that new galaxies form to fill the gaps left by galaxies moving away, so the universe looks the same over time.
Dr. Bondi suggested that only a small amount of matter needs to be created, such as a single hydrogen atom in a living room-sized area every few million years.
He also claimed that this idea does not contradict the principle of conservation of matter and energy because some error is likely in such experiments.
Dr. Lyttleton proposed a different theory, suggesting that the universe is electric in nature.
He focused on the behavior of protons and electrons, which have opposite charges and attract each other to form hydrogen atoms.
Dr. Lyttleton questioned whether the charges of protons and electrons are exactly equal.
If protons have a slightly greater charge, this would give hydrogen atoms a slight charge-excess.
He imagined the universe as a large hydrogen sphere, where surface atoms shoot away due to the strong electrical forces.
This, he argued, could explain the observed expansion of the universe.
The book summarizing these discussions, called 'Rival Theories Of Cosmology,' offers a glimpse into how scientists think about the cosmos.
It includes photographs and charts to help non-scientists understand the theories.
The scientists expressed hope that future space-based telescopes would help test and refine their theories.
Currently, the Earth's atmosphere blocks many important observations, especially in the ultraviolet range.
They believe that a telescope above the atmosphere could provide crucial data to support or challenge existing theories.
Despite the complexity of the universe, scientists continue to search for answers using the best tools available.
The missile race, while driven by conflict, may also help advance space exploration.
In doing so, it provides a new way to study the universe and understand our place in it.
stem: According to the passage, which of the following is true?

options.A: The universe is currently contracting because galaxies are moving closer together.
options.B: Dr. Bondi argued that the steady-state theory requires the destruction of existing galaxies.
options.C: Missile technology may provide the means for launching spacecraft into orbit.
options.D: Protons definitely have a greater charge than electrons, according to Dr. Lyttleton.
